Every other way to split them

Every figure on this page is built from two numbers. The level is how strong a player is. The map effect is how much a particular map suits them, better or worse than their own average. Add the two and you get the Est Elo — the dot in panel C, the cell on Balance, the side's three in Versus. Sections 1 to 8 are how those two are produced; 9 and 10 are the two readings that a single number cannot give.

The raw material is public match history: every game these players have played since 2021, ranked and lobby, each record carrying the rating all ten players held at the moment they played it.

1 · The win rate is thrown away

Matchmaking hands you opponents of your own strength, so almost everybody sits near 50% however good they are. A win rate says the ladder is working; it does not say who is good.

What separates players is who they beat. So every game is priced by the opposition that was in it.

2 · How strong the opposition was

O = own rating + (enemy team average − own team average)

In a 1v1 that is just the opponent's rating. In a team game it credits a player for the help they had and charges them for the carry they did: play beside weaker allies and O goes up, hide behind stronger ones and it goes down.

3 · The rating that would explain the record

Elo has one formula. The chance a player rated R beats an opponent rated O is

E = 1 / (1 + 10(O − R) / 400)

400 points of gap is ten-to-one odds; 100 points is about 64%.

The performance rating is the rating that would make the record unremarkable — the R at which the expected wins come out equal to the real ones:

E₁ + E₂ + … + En = wins

Where every opponent happens to be the same strength this has a short form worth keeping in your head:

R = O + 400 × log₁₀(wins / losses) 7–3 against 1600s → 1600 + 400 × log₁₀(2.33) = 1747

4 · Measured against the player's own average

A performance rating is an absolute number, so it moves when a player improves. Games four years apart cannot simply be subtracted. Everything is therefore measured relative to the player's own rating in those same games:

edge = R − (their average rating while playing them)

The map's effect is then that edge on the map, minus the edge on every other map in the pool.

Two traps hide in that sentence. Both were live mistakes here, and both changed who the tables recommended:

  • Leave the map out of its own baseline. Compare a map against an average it is part of and the answer shrinks by exactly the map's share of the sample. A player with 96% of his games on one map would report an effect of zero by construction.
  • Subtract the rating of the day, not of today. Otherwise a map played during a bad year scores as a bad map. Before this was fixed, 85% of the gap between a player's form then and now was flowing straight into the map number.

5 · Believed only as far as the sample allows

Anything measured on twelve games is mostly luck. Each number arrives with a standard error, and is pulled toward zero in proportion to how much of it could be noise:

shown = raw × τ² / (τ² + se²)

τ is how far map skill really does vary from map to map, once the measurement error has been taken back out. It is re-measured for every roster and printed on the Teams tab — about 70 Elo.

A wide error bar drives the factor toward zero and the cell falls back to the player's level; a narrow one lets nearly the whole raw number through.

Every figure on the page carries what is left of that error, and none of them carries it as a verdict. There used to be a column of ✔ and ✱ marks saying whether a cell was "real" at two standard errors; it is gone, because a threshold printed beside a number is read as the number being true or false, and what the arithmetic supports is a range. So the error is drawn instead — the bar on every dot in panel C, the width of the ribbon in E, the length of the ±1 and ±2 bars in A — and the reader sees how much room there is rather than being told the answer.

6 · The level is a fit over results, not a ladder rating

A ladder rating is the obvious place to get a level from, and it was where this one came from until 2026-09-28. It is not where it comes from now, and the reason is that a team rating is settled by the team: a carried player floats above their own contribution and a carrying one sits below it, and no amount of correcting a number after the fact gets inside the games that made it.

So the level is solved from the results directly. One strength per player, fitted over 31 253 matches at once, so that the stronger side tends to win — the same shape as section 3, but over the whole field instead of one player, so everybody's strength is estimated against everybody else's at the same time:

maximise   Σ log P(the side that won, won) P from the same Elo curve, on the two sides' mean strengths

The player's own published rating is never used to rate them. It is used for everyone in a game who is not in this field — an opponent has to be priced somehow — but the thing being solved for is never anchored to the thing it is meant to check.

Shrunk toward the field, by the same rule as section 5: a player with four games does not get a strength four games can carry, they get the field's average moved as far as four games earns. The prior is a Gaussian on the field mean with its width stated in Elo (250), which is a claim anybody can argue with — it replaced a bare coefficient that shrank by an amount nobody could state.

The team lift

The fit above pools 1v1 and team games. A player who is better in team games than at 1v1 would be read almost entirely off their 1v1 record, so a second fit is run on team games only, and the pooled level is lifted toward it — never lowered — by how much of the disagreement survives both error bars:

lift = max(team-only − pooled − offset, 0) × τ² / (τ² + se²)

Never lowered because the asymmetry is the point: being good in team games is the thing this page is for, and a team-only fit that reads below the pooled one is as likely to be its own thinner sample talking.

7 · What a 1v1 game says about a team player

The two boards are pooled, so something has to say how far a 1v1 result reaches across into a team rating. Two separate things do, and conflating them was a real mistake here:

  • How much it is worth, in points. A result constrains the whole side, so what it says about any one player in it falls as the square of the side's size: against one 1v1 game, a 2v2 is worth an eighth, a 3v3 an eighteenth and a 4v4 a thirty-third. That is arithmetic, not a choice.
  • How far it reaches, across formats. That is a different question and it has a different answer: a 1v1 result is evidence about 1v1 strength, and only partly about the same person in a 4v4. It is trusted at 10% when the two boards are mixed.

Both at full weight, the median row of this field was 82% 1v1 information — a team ranking mostly inferred from 1v1 play. At 10% that is 32%, measured at no cost in accuracy on held-out team games. 0% is worse, so the 1v1 board must not simply be switched off: it is the only reading of a player that a stack cannot distort.

Panel B on Players and Compare is this split, per row. The upper bar is where the fit's information about that player came from — team against 1v1, after both weights above — so a pale bar is a team ranking resting on 1v1 games. The lower bar is how much of their team play was with one partner: past 55% the fit cannot tell the pair apart, and the row is closer to the partnership's strength than to the player's.

Recency. Only the last 180 days are fitted, at full weight; a player with under 20 equivalent games there reaches back through their older games, newest first, until they have that much.

8 · Est Elo, per map

Est Elo = level + map effect

The map effect is read down three rungs, and each one moves the estimate only as far as its own sample earns it. The level is where every cell starts. The map's group — Open, Closed, Water and so on, with this map's own games taken out of it — moves it from there. Then the map's own record moves it again. So a cell on nine games is not thrown away and a cell on four hundred is not held back, and a map nobody here has played still has its category underneath it.

What the mark after a number means, which is simply which rung got the last word. It is printed on Balance; panel C of Compare and Teams says the same thing with a filled dot, a hollow one and a dashed bar:

(none)the player's own record on that map moved it off its category
°only the category could move it — too little on this map to say anything beyond what its neighbours already said. The games count in the tooltip is still games on that map, which is how you see how thin the reading is
~neither could: the figure is the player's own level, and the bar on it is the whole spread of map effects

Then an inexperience penalty, charged on how much of what the map is made of the player has played — −100 Elo at none of it, sliding to nothing at 20 games. It is measured rather than assumed: players really do underperform their rating on a kind of map they have barely played. The count is never the map's own, because somebody with three hundred Arena games is not a novice on Michi.

A map is a composition, not a category, so the charge is too. Border Dispute is four-fifths open and a fifth laming, and a player's charge on it is four-fifths of what their open experience costs plus a fifth of what their laming experience costs. A game counts toward an aspect by its map's share of that aspect, so a thousand games of Black Forest — a tenth laming — is a hundred games of laming experience. Read as a category instead, a career of Arabia bought nothing on an open map filed under Laming.

The Inexp column is the same charge over the whole event, which is one composition like any map: every aspect's charge, weighted by the share of the event that aspect is, and those shares sum to 1. So a player who has played none of anything pays the whole 100, and one who knows everything but water, at a tenth of the event, pays ten. It is a summary of the cells and not a second charge — the maps' own figures carry theirs already, and nothing adds this to a level.

There is no inexperience penalty. One was charged until 2026-09-17 — up to 100 Elo on a kind of map the player had barely touched, on the reasoning that a thin cell rests on a level earned somewhere else. It was dropped because it does not predict: scored on games it had never seen, pooled over every roster, it is worth −0.04 to +0.04 thousandths of a nat on three different holdouts that disagree in sign, against map models worth 1 to 5 on the same scale. It was moving published Elo by up to 90 on an eighth of the cells, and no test could show that it helped.

Every cell carries an error bar, at two standard errors, so about 95% of the time — drawn in panel C and printed in every hover. One thing it does not say: it is the bar on the shrunk figure, so the width says how far the printed number could move, not how much is known about the map — that is the games count. The widest belong to the ~ cells, where the bar is the spread of map effects itself: we do not know this map.

Everything here is on the team-ladder scale, which reads a few hundred points below the 1v1 rating of the same person. Do not compare an Est Elo to a 1v1 Elo.

9 · The curve: who they meet, and who they beat

Everything above produces one number per player per map. Panel E answers a question one number cannot: is this player better against strong opposition or weak? A level says where somebody sits; it cannot say whether they hold up against the top of the field or feast on the bottom of it.

It is section 3 again — the rating that would make the record unremarkable — but solved at thirty places along the opposition axis rather than once over everything. Each place weights the games near it and ignores the rest:

w = (1 − (|opposition − here| / h)³)³   inside h, and 0 beyond it × 0.5^(days ago / half-life)   and 0 past the cut

The first term is distance in Elo, the second is age. They multiply, so a point is drawn from games near in opposition and near in time.

h is adaptive: it reaches out to the nearest 30% of that player's games, measured in weight rather than in count, so the window is narrow where they played a lot and opens up where the games run out instead of collapsing onto three of them.

Why a line and not an average

The obvious thing is to average the window. That is wrong at the ends, and badly. An average reports the level over its whole window, so wherever the curve slopes it is pulled toward the middle of the range — and at the top, where the window has games only on one side, there is nothing on the far side to pull it back. On a real row that was 177 Elo of the interior leaking into the top. So each place is fitted as a local line through its window and the line's height at that Elo is drawn.

The obvious fix — count only games at or above each point — costs more than it saves: it reads the top of the range on a third of the evidence and the very top on none at all. Measured, and rejected.

How much is behind a point

Not the number of games, which under two sets of weights means nothing, but the effective count:

neff = (Σw)² / Σw²

A hundred games worth a twentieth each are not a hundred games, and this is the figure that says so. It is what the error bar is built from, and it is what decides the marker: filled above 30, hollow below it, and no point at all below 10 — a gap in the line is a gap, not a guess. The exposure panel underneath counts in the same currency, so a band and a point are the same kind of figure.

The shaded area is that point's own ±1 standard error, from the weighted profile likelihood. It prices the estimate at Σw games where the true sampling error is the smaller sandwich, so it errs about 10% wide — toward saying less. What it does not carry is smoothing bias: where the true curve bends, the arm is honest about noise and silent about that.

⚠ Neighbouring points share games, so a wiggle narrower than the local window is the kernel moving and not the player. And on the team board this is one player's share of a side result, so it moves by the side's size: a 4v4 surplus takes four times the individual rating a 1v1 one would, and the error bar is four times as wide with it.

The half-life, and why it is not a window

This was a hard window until 2026-09-29 — the last n days at full weight and nothing before. A window is a step nobody picked the date of: a game 182 days old counts in full, one 184 days old counts for nothing, and inside the window last week and five months ago count the same.

The reason there is a cut-off as well is measured, and it is the half that is easy to leave out. A pure decay is worse than the window it replaces, because its tail is exactly the old games carrying the old rating — and in ranked matchmaking you meet your own level, so a player's opposition axis is very nearly their own rating over time. Over the 89 players with twelve or more rated ranked team games, as the median correlation between a game's opposition and the rating its player held then:

hard window 183d90 effective games60/89 drawable 0.42
pure half-life 90d15281/890.52
half-life 90d, cut at 365d12573/89 0.45

So the shipped default has 39% more evidence than the window it replaced, 13 more players with any curve at all, and no more of the confound. The cut is at four half-lives, where a game is down to a sixteenth.

10 · Tiers, because the order is finer than the evidence

The field sorts into a ranking, and a ranking invites being read place by place. It does not support that. Measured on this field, not one adjacent pair in it is separated by more than its combined standard error — so 87 places are 87 claims the data does not make.

A tier breaks where a player falls more than one combined standard error below the player leading the tier — against the leader and not the row above, or a long shallow run joins two ends that are plainly apart. The rules down panel A are where they break, and the order inside one of them is not a ranking.

11 · What is thrown away

  • anything under 8 minutes — those are drops, not games
  • anything that is not a classic random map: Empire Wars, Return of Rome, treaty, regicide, deathmatch, data mods, scenarios, altered resources
  • every map outside the tournament pool
  • lobby games whose name announces a format this tournament is not — 1v1, ffa, 3v3v3, shared control
  • games from before the mid-2022 team-ladder rescale, spotted by a recorded rating above the player's own all-time peak
  • the unranked rating a lobby game carries — each player's ranked rating is looked up instead

Lobby games also come in about 6.6 percentage points below what their ratings predict, because self-picked teams are far more lopsided than matchmaking. So ranked and lobby games are kept in separate pools, each with its own baseline, and combined afterwards. They can compare one map against another; they cannot speak to absolute level.

12 · What these numbers cannot do

  • One map cell is weak evidence. Measure a map on the first half of a career and again on the second, and the two agree at only 0.28. Under about 25 games read the direction only; under 10 nothing works at all, which is why those cells fall back to the level.
  • Nothing reaches a map never played. A group is often one big map wearing another map's name. The ° is there so that is never invisible.
  • The anchor leans high. Half of it is a peak, and a peak is the top of a noisy series. It is applied to everyone alike, so comparisons hold, but absolute levels are optimistic.
  • The seat is read off the colour, and only in ranked games. Ranked hands out position by colour — the colours run round the map and a team takes the odd ones or the even ones — so ordering a side by colour gives its arc, whose two ends border an opponent and whose middle is pocket. A lobby assigns no colours, so there the player number is the seat. Neither is the start position itself, which the match record does not carry, and on a nomad map there is no flank or pocket to read at all.
  • A rating measures what the ladder measured. Nobody here has a record of playing as this particular four, on a stage, against a team that prepared for them.

The full argument, with the measurement behind every rule, is in method.md; whether to believe any of it — the estimator scored against an arbiter that reads nobody's own ladder rating — is in validity.md.

Compare, Versus and Teams are locked

The player-by-player and roster-by-roster readings are behind a password. The password is checked here in the browser, off the file itself — nothing is sent anywhere, and the rest of the page needs no password at all.
